summary: The Legal Aid Society reports from NYPD records that the Facial Identification Section first returned no match in a public-lewdness investigation, after which the Special Activities Unit produced a possible facial-recognition match to Trevis Williams. Legal Aid states that Williams did not match the victim's physical description but was arrested after the later match and a disputed identification procedure; it also says his life and job prospects were put on hold. AIID describes more than two days in custody; CBS reports that Williams spent two days in custody, was charged with an indecent-exposure offence, and that the case was later dismissed. Williams described continuing stress and fear that he might have been required to register as a sex offender. NYPD told CBS that facial recognition was used only as a possible lead and stated its general policy against arrest solely on a facial-recognition match.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Legal Aid reports from its review of NYPD records that FIS first returned no match for surveillance material in a public-lewdness investigation; hours later a possible match was entered that Legal Aid says came from the Special Activities Unit rather than FIS. Legal Aid states that the later match identified Trevis Williams even though he did not match the victim's physical description, and that the match was followed by an identification procedure and arrest. AIID describes more than two days in custody; CBS reports that Williams spent two days in custody, was charged with indecent exposure and that the case was later dismissed. Williams told CBS that the experience remained very stressful and that he continued to think about the possibility that he could have been required to register as a sex offender. Legal Aid also states that his life and job prospects were put on hold. NYPD told CBS that facial recognition was only a possible lead and stated its general policy against arrest solely on a match. The CBS response does not supply the case-specific corroboration record.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: This occurrence combines inferential-authority risk with a material provenance discontinuity. An initial no-match did not end the inquiry; a different unit later produced a possible match whose method, database and approval basis remain unclear in the public record. That later inference selected Williams for a downstream identification pathway despite a material mismatch with the victim's description. Legal Aid disputes the independence and adequacy of the later identification procedure, while NYPD’s reported response states a general policy against arrest solely on a facial match. The cited response does not document the actual probable-cause evidence. The preserved evidence therefore supports an ambiguous Inferential Evidence–Authority Separation boundary finding rather than a failure occurrence. The invariant remains that a probabilistic identity inference must stay provisional until the downstream evidentiary basis and contradictory checks are sufficient for the contemplated coercive effect. The preserved competing accounts leave the independence and sufficiency of downstream identification unresolved; they support the existing ambiguous boundaries, without proving either an inference-only arrest or an invariant success. Independent external review retains evidentiary boundaries for contemporaneous validation, uncertainty, population/bias assessment and investigative reliability propositions where the decisive implementation or documentation record is unavailable. Requirements published after the occurrence or addressing different statutory, generative-model, content-provenance or safety-function objects are excluded to the audit. These outcomes do not depend on voluntary-standard adoption and do not determine the disputed legal claims.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: This incident demonstrates that contestability requires both evidentiary independence and provenance. A consequential identity inference should carry enough lineage to show which unit generated it, against what authorised source set, by what method and under what approval, especially when it contradicts an earlier search. Decision-makers should also be required to document which downstream evidence arose independently of the machine nomination and which contradictions were actively resolved before arrest or detention.
